Khapre RV.lab_name: Kondratov Lab, Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease, Cleveland State University (Cleveland, Ohio, USA)
Khapre RV.role: Circadian biologist who did her PhD in Roman Kondratov's lab at Cleveland State University, where she showed that the clock protein BMAL1 acts as a brake on mTORC1 and that feeding times set a daily rhythm in mTORC1 activity
Khapre RV.sub: Postdoctoral fellow, Cleveland Clinic (listed by the Kondratov lab; 2016 paper from the Lerner Research Institute) · PhD student, Kondratov lab, Cleveland State University (2009–2014)
story: The body runs on a roughly 24-hour internal clock, and the protein BMAL1 is one of its core gears. Mice that lack BMAL1 age early and die young. In the Atlas study KHA2014, Khapre and colleagues asked whether this early ageing runs through mTORC1, the growth-control complex that rapamycin blocks. In mouse tissues and in cultured cells without BMAL1, mTORC1 was more active than normal. When Bmal1 knockout mice were given rapamycin, their lifespan rose by about 50 percent. The result places the clock upstream of mTORC1 as a brake, and suggests that losing that brake is part of why these mice age fast. It is a mouse and cell result, not a human one.

A companion paper from the same year, with Khapre as first author, found that mTORC1 activity in mouse tissues rises and falls on a 24-hour rhythm that is set by feeding times, not by light, and keeps going during fasting. The authors proposed that this food-driven rhythm is a second clock that runs alongside the light-driven one. An earlier first-author paper (2011) showed more senescent cells in the tissues of Bmal1 knockout mice and linked BMAL1 to how cells handle oxidative stress.

Khapre trained as a PhD student in Roman Kondratov's lab at Cleveland State University from 2009 to 2014, according to the lab's alumni list. The same list names her current post as a postdoctoral fellow at Cleveland Clinic, and a 2016 paper lists her at the Neuroinflammation Research Center of the Lerner Research Institute there, on a study of memory loss after brain bleeding in mice. No more recent position could be confirmed.

highlights.KHA2014: First author: showed in mice and cells that loss of the clock protein BMAL1 raises mTORC1 activity, and that rapamycin lengthens the life of Bmal1 knockout mice by about 50 percent.

Khapre RV.note: Current position after 2016 not confirmed; the Kondratov lab alumni page says postdoctoral fellow at Cleveland Clinic (page date unknown). lab_name kept at the Atlas-paper affiliation. The lab page uses 'she'.

Wu JJ.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Center for Molecular Medicine, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Wu JJ.role: Researcher in Toren Finkel's laboratory at the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and first author of the 2013 study showing that mice making only a quarter of the normal amount of mTOR live about 20 percent longer
Wu JJ.sub: Center for Molecular Medicine, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, NIH (Toren Finkel lab, papers 2009–2013, at the time of the study)
story: Rapamycin lengthens the life of mice, but a drug can have side effects that muddy the picture. In the Atlas study WUX2013, Wu and colleagues in Toren Finkel's lab at the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute took a genetic route instead. They bred mice that make only about 25 percent of the normal amount of mTOR protein. These mice lived about 20 percent longer on average: median lifespan was 28.0 versus 22.9 months in males and 31.5 versus 26.5 months in females.

The slowing of ageing was uneven, which is why the paper calls it segmental and tissue-specific. The mTOR-reduced mice kept better memory and balance in old age, but they lost more bone and were more prone to infection. For the Atlas this is a clean mouse experiment showing that turning mTOR down, not off, can extend life, and that the benefit does not reach every organ.

PubMed lists Wu on several papers with Finkel between 2009 and 2013, including work on Wnt signalling and liver glucose metabolism, and on two studies with Elizabeth Henske's group at Brigham and Women's Hospital on autophagy in tuberous sclerosis complex, a disease in which mTORC1 is overactive. Wu's current position could not be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.WUX2013: First author: led the study of mice engineered to make about a quarter of the normal amount of mTOR, which lived about 20 percent longer with a tissue-by-tissue pattern of slower ageing.

Oki T.lab_name: Center for Regenerative Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Oki T.role: Hematology researcher who trained at the Institute of Medical Science in Tokyo and in David Scadden's lab at Massachusetts General Hospital, where he imaged mTORC1 activity in leukemia cells inside living mice
Oki T.sub: Center for Regenerative Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Stem Cell Institute (David Scadden lab, papers 2021–2023) · Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo (Toshio Kitamura lab, papers to 2014)
story: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. In the Atlas study OKI2021, Oki and colleagues built fluorescent reporters that light up when mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is active, and watched AML cells inside the bone marrow of living mice. mTORC1 activity in the leukemia cells fell as the disease advanced. But at the moment chemotherapy was working best, mTORC1 switched back on in the surviving cells, and this was a change inside the cells rather than the survival of a pre-existing group. Blocking mTORC1 at exactly that time killed more AML cells.

The point for the Atlas is timing. mTORC1 activity is not a fixed property of a tumour; it shifts over days, and a drug given at the wrong time may do little. The work was done in mice and has not been tested as a treatment schedule in patients.

PubMed shows Oki working on leukemia biology at the Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo, in Toshio Kitamura's division up to 2014, then at the Center for Regenerative Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Harvard Stem Cell Institute with David Scadden, where he also contributed to a 2023 study of cartilage repair cells.

highlights.OKI2021: First author: imaged mTORC1 activity in AML cells in the bone marrow of living mice and showed that inhibiting mTORC1 at the peak of chemotherapy response improved killing.

Oki T.note: Current affiliation (AbbVie) rests on one 2026 PubMed record with the same full name in the same field (hematologic cancer); no official page seen. Please confirm or revert lab_name to the MGH Center for Regenerative Medicine (Boston, Massachusetts, USA).

Abdul-Azees PA.lab_name: Center for Regenerative Sciences and Department of Comprehensive Dentistry, School of Dentistry, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Abdul-Azees PA.role: Oral biology researcher at the UT Health San Antonio School of Dentistry who works on dental caries, oral biofilms and salivary gland ageing, and first author of the marmoset study of rapamycin and the ageing salivary gland
Abdul-Azees PA.sub: Center for Regenerative Sciences and Department of Comprehensive Dentistry, School of Dentistry, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2023–2026)
story: Older people often have a dry mouth because their salivary glands shrink and scar. In the Atlas study ABD2026, Abdul-Azees, Chih-Ko Yeh and colleagues looked at the submandibular salivary gland of the common marmoset, a small primate that ages much faster than humans. Older glands had fewer of the cells that make saliva, more duct and scar-like connective tissue, more fat build-up and more dying and senescent (permanently arrested) cells. Marmosets given rapamycin by mouth for a long period kept more of the saliva-making structure and showed less scarring and fat build-up.

Rapamycin blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The study suggests that some age-related damage in a primate gland can be slowed by this drug. It was a tissue study in a small number of animals and was not tested in people.

On PubMed, Abdul-Azees first appears in 2023 in Bennett Amaechi's group in the Department of Comprehensive Dentistry at UT Health San Antonio, on a laboratory model of tooth decay (an artificial mouth) and later on toothpaste formulas that prevent caries. Since 2025 the papers carry the Center for Regenerative Sciences affiliation with Chih-Ko Yeh and Xiao-Dong Chen, including work on how bacterial biofilms grow on dental filling materials.

highlights.ABD2026: First author: described how the marmoset salivary gland changes with age and found partial preservation of gland structure with long-term oral rapamycin.

Lee SY.lab_name: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science, and Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST (Daejeon, South Korea)
Lee SY.role: Neuroscientist in Won-Suk Chung's group at KAIST and the Institute for Basic Science who studies how neurons, astrocytes and immune cells interact in Alzheimer's disease, and first author of the 2026 Nature study on ERBB4 in excitatory neurons
Lee SY.sub: Senior researcher, Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (2026) · Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST (Won-Suk Chung group, papers 2024–2026)
story: In Alzheimer's disease, brain circuits become unbalanced long before memory fails. In the Atlas study LEE2026, Lee and colleagues in Won-Suk Chung's group found that the receptor protein ERBB4 turns up in a group of excitatory (signal-sending) neurons very early in Alzheimer's model mice. Removing ERBB4 from these neurons reduced synapse loss, inflammation from support cells called glia, amyloid plaques and memory problems. Putting ERBB4 into the excitatory neurons of healthy mice was enough to cause synapse loss, glial inflammation and memory problems, though not plaques. These effects needed mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

For the Atlas, the study adds a new route into mTOR in the brain: a receptor that appears in the wrong cell type and drives damage through mTOR. The causal experiments were done in mice. The team also reported higher ERBB4 in excitatory neurons in human brain tissue from people with Alzheimer's disease, which is an association, not proof of cause.

On PubMed, Lee has worked with Chung at the Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST, including a 2024 review on how astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells of the brain, talk to neurons, blood vessels and immune cells, and a 2025 study with collaborators in Bonn on the receptor Tyro3 and brain inflammation in Alzheimer's models. Korean press coverage of the Nature paper describes Lee as a senior researcher who led the study at the Institute for Basic Science Center for Vascular Research, where Chung is deputy director.

highlights.LEE2026: First author: showed in mice that ERBB4 switched on in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's-like synapse loss, inflammation and memory decline through mTOR signalling.

Lee SY.note: Position 'senior researcher' comes from a Korean newspaper report (Herald), not an official page. Common name (Lee): identity tied by KAIST plus co-author Won-Suk Chung.

De Nardi A.lab_name: Centre for Computational and Systems Biology (COSBI), Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento (Rovereto, Italy)
De Nardi A.role: Mathematical modeller in Trento who applies survival and epidemic models to medical data, and first author of the 2026 re-analysis of the RAP-ALS rapamycin trial in ALS
De Nardi A.sub: COSBI, Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento (2026)
story: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease in which the nerve cells that control muscles die. RAP-ALS was a small clinical trial of rapamycin, the drug that blocks the growth-control complex mTORC1, in people with ALS. In the Atlas study DEN2026B, De Nardi and colleagues went back to the trial data (63 patients) and asked which factors predicted survival. Among carriers of a mutation in the C9orf72 gene, the most common genetic cause of ALS, those treated with rapamycin survived longer, and the same pattern held against a separate group of 40 C9orf72 carriers.

This is a secondary, exploratory analysis. The number of treated C9orf72 carriers was small, and the patients were not randomised for this question, so the drug may not be the cause of the difference. The result is a reason for a proper trial in this genetic group, not evidence that rapamycin works in ALS.
PubMed lists De Nardi in 2026 at COSBI in Rovereto, a computational biology centre run jointly by Microsoft Research and the University of Trento.

highlights.DEN2026B: First author: re-analysed RAP-ALS trial survival and found a possible survival benefit of rapamycin in C9orf72 mutation carriers, flagged as exploratory.

De Nardi A.note: Only two PubMed records. The 2024 Trento mathematics paper is linked by name and Trento location plus modelling field, not by a shared co-author; moderate confidence. No official page found (web search budget ran out).

Simpson SJ.lab_name: Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, The University of Sydney (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia)
Simpson SJ.role: Biologist who began with how locusts choose their food and is known for the Geometric Framework for nutrition, which shows that the balance of protein, carbohydrate and fat shapes health and lifespan; inaugural academic director of the Charles Perkins Centre
Simpson SJ.sub: Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, The University of Sydney · Executive director, Obesity Australia (since 2018) · Inaugural academic director, Charles Perkins Centre (2014–2025) · ARC Federation Fellow, University of Sydney (from 2005) · about 22 years at the University of Oxford · PhD, King's College London (1982) · BSc, University of Queensland (1978)
story: Is it how much we eat, or what we eat, that sets how long we live? In the Atlas study SOL2014, Simpson's group, with first author Samantha Solon-Biet, fed mice 25 diets that differed in protein, carbohydrate, fat and energy content and let them eat freely for life. Total calories did not decide lifespan or metabolic health. The ratio of protein to carbohydrate did: mice on low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets lived longest, and they also had lower mTOR activation in the liver. The study links diet composition to mTOR, the nutrient sensor that rapamycin blocks. It was done in mice.

Simpson studied at the University of Queensland (BSc, 1978) and earned a PhD at King's College London in 1982 on how locust nymphs control their food intake. He then spent about 22 years at the University of Oxford, in Experimental Psychology, Zoology and the University Museum of Natural History. His group, with colleagues including David Raubenheimer, uses the Geometric Framework (nutritional geometry), a way of mapping how animals balance several nutrients at once.

He returned to Australia in 2005 as an ARC Federation Fellow at the University of Sydney and served as the inaugural academic director of the Charles Perkins Centre from 2014 to 2025. Since 2018 he has also been executive director of Obesity Australia. He is a Fellow of the Royal Society (2013) and of the Australian Academy of Science (2007), and a Companion of the Order of Australia (2016).

highlights.SOL2014: Senior author: led the 25-diet mouse study showing that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio, not calorie intake, shaped lifespan and metabolic health, with lower liver mTOR activation on low-protein diets.

Bannister CA.lab_name: Human Data Sciences (Cardiff, Wales, United Kingdom)
Bannister CA.role: Health data analyst from Craig Currie's group in Cardiff who works with UK primary care records, and first author of the 2014 comparison of survival in people with type 2 diabetes on metformin and people without diabetes
Bannister CA.sub: Human Data Sciences, Cardiff (PubMed affiliation, 2023) · Cochrane Institute of Primary Care and Public Health, School of Medicine, Cardiff University (papers 2013–2018)
story: Metformin is the most common first drug for type 2 diabetes, and it is being studied as a possible anti-ageing drug, partly because it acts on cell energy sensing that feeds into mTOR. In the Atlas study BAN2014, Bannister, Craig Currie and colleagues used UK primary care records to compare people with type 2 diabetes who started on metformin, people who started on a sulphonylurea, and matched people without diabetes. Those started on metformin had slightly longer median survival than the matched non-diabetic group, while those on sulphonylureas had shorter survival.

The study is observational. People prescribed metformin may differ from others in ways the records do not capture, and people who keep taking their medicine tend to be healthier in other ways too, so the result is consistent with a benefit but does not prove one.

On PubMed, Bannister's papers from 2013 to 2018 come from Cardiff University with Currie, using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, a large UK database of anonymised GP records. They include a 2013 study showing that a widely used heart risk calculator for diabetes overestimated risk. A 2023 paper lists Bannister at Human Data Sciences in Cardiff, a company working on an online platform that turns routine health records into disease statistics.

highlights.BAN2014: First author: analysed UK primary care records and found that people with type 2 diabetes started on metformin had slightly longer survival than matched people without diabetes.

Xie J.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources, College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (Tai'an, Shandong, China)
Xie J.role: Animal nutrition researcher in Ning Jiao's group at Shandong Agricultural University who studies how feed contaminants damage the pig gut, and first author of the piglet study on glutamine and bisphenol A
Xie J.sub: College of Animal Science and Technology, Shandong Agricultural University (Ning Jiao group, papers 2026)
story: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial chemical found in some plastics that can reach animal feed. In the Atlas study XIE2026, Xie, Ning Jiao and colleagues fed piglets BPA and found damage to the jejunum, the middle part of the small intestine. Adding the amino acid glutamine to the feed reduced the damage, helped the gut lining stay sealed and restored how the cells' mitochondria produce energy. These changes came with shifts in AMPK and mTOR signalling, the two linked sensors of cell energy and nutrients.
The study shows an association between glutamine, gut repair and AMPK-mTOR signalling in pigs. It does not prove that the mTOR change causes the protection, and it was not done in people.

PubMed lists Xie only in 2026, both times in Jiao's group at the Key Laboratory of Efficient Utilization of Non-grain Feed Resources at Shandong Agricultural University in Tai'an. The second paper looked at how the mould toxin zearalenone and its hidden glucoside form harm pig intestinal cells. The career stage (student or staff) could not be confirmed.

highlights.XIE2026: First author: showed in piglets that glutamine reduced bisphenol A damage to the small intestine, with restored mitochondrial energy production and changes in AMPK-mTOR signalling.

Li G.lab_name: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (Yantai, China)
Li G.role: Researcher at the College of Life Sciences, Yantai University, and senior author of a mouse study of the plant compound pungenin and hair regrowth
Li G.sub: College of Life Sciences, Yantai University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Androgenetic alopecia is the common pattern hair loss driven by male hormones. A hormone called DHT shrinks hair follicles, and the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT from testosterone. In the Atlas study ZHAI2026, Li's group, with first author Wencai Zhai, treated mice with DHT to cause hair loss and then applied pungenin, a compound found in plants, to the skin. Hair grew back faster, the follicles made less type II 5-alpha-reductase, and genes in the PI3K/AKT/FoxO/mTOR pathway, which controls cell growth and survival, changed their activity in hair follicle cells.
The mTOR link in this study comes from gene activity measurements in mice, not from blocking or activating mTOR directly, so it shows association rather than cause. It has not been tested in people.
Gang Li is a very common name, and no other publication or official page could be tied to this person with confidence. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

Piatkevich KD.lab_name: Piatkevich Lab, School of Life Sciences, Westlake University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Piatkevich KD.role: Protein engineer who designs fluorescent proteins and biosensors for imaging cells and brains, trained with Vladislav Verkhusha and Edward Boyden, now running a lab at Westlake University
Piatkevich KD.sub: Principal investigator, School of Life Sciences, Westlake University, Hangzhou (papers to 2026) · Media Lab, MIT (Edward Boyden lab, papers around 2018) · Department of Anatomy and Structural Biology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine (Vladislav Verkhusha lab, papers 2009–2014)
story: Most ways of measuring mTOR activity give a snapshot: you break open the cells at one moment and look. In the Atlas study WANG2026C, Piatkevich's lab built a fluorescent protein ticker tape, a set of self-assembling protein fibres that grow inside a cell and lay down fluorescent colour bands over time, like rings in a tree trunk. Each colour can be tied to the activity of a different signalling pathway, including mTOR, NF-kB, STAT3, NFAT and cAMP. Reading the bands later gives a history of each pathway in each single cell, in culture and in living animals.

Using the mTOR version, the team saw mTOR activity rise and fall in step with the cell division cycle. That supports the idea that mTOR signalling is dynamic, not a fixed on or off state, which is one of the Atlas's current themes. The recording was done in cells and animals, not in people.

On PubMed, Piatkevich's first papers (from 2009) come from Vladislav Verkhusha's lab at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York, on fluorescent timers that change colour as proteins age and on red fluorescent proteins with unusual colour properties. By 2018 the papers come from Edward Boyden's group at the MIT Media Lab, including Archon1, a fluorescent voltage reporter for imaging electrical activity in neurons, found with a robotic cell-picking screen. Recent papers come from Piatkevich's own group at the School of Life Sciences, Westlake University, in Hangzhou, on far-red fluorescent proteins and super-resolution imaging, and the Atlas paper also lists Zhejiang University.

highlights.WANG2026C: Senior author: led the development of the fluorescent protein ticker tape that records the history of mTOR and other pathways in single cells and showed mTOR activity oscillating with the cell cycle.

Piatkevich KD.note: No lab page opened (web search budget ran out); lab_url omitted. Atlas paper affiliation is Zhejiang University; 2026 papers list Westlake University as corresponding address, so lab_name changed to Westlake. PhD institution not confirmed from a source (Albert Einstein papers may be PhD or postdoc). 'Principal investigator' inferred from corresponding-author role on 2026 papers.

Jin P.lab_name: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University (Chongqing, China)
Jin P.role: Pharmaceutical scientist in Lei Luo's group at Southwest University in Chongqing who studies the drug pump P-glycoprotein, and first author of the study showing that oxidative stress boosts P-glycoprotein production through mTOR
Jin P.sub: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, Chongqing (Lei Luo group, papers 2025–2026)
story: P-glycoprotein is a pump in the cell membrane that throws drugs back out of the cell. Cancer cells that make a lot of it can resist many drugs at once. In the Atlas study JIN2026, Jin and colleagues in Lei Luo's group showed in cells that oxidative stress (a build-up of reactive oxygen molecules) switches on a chain of signals, PI3K to AKT to mTORC1 to the RNA-unwinding protein eIF4A, that makes the cell translate more P-glycoprotein from its existing messenger RNA. Because this skips the slower step of making new RNA, it is a fast route to drug resistance.
For the Atlas, the study is an example of mTORC1 acting through eIF4A to pick which proteins get made. It was done in cultured cells; whether it happens in tumours in patients is not shown.

On PubMed, Jin works with Luo at the College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, on how drugs are absorbed and pumped out of cells. Earlier papers in the group include a 2025 study showing that glucosamine directly switches on intestinal P-glycoprotein and reduces drug absorption, and a 2026 study on making the colorectal cancer drug trifluridine better absorbed when taken by mouth. Career stage could not be confirmed.

highlights.JIN2026: First author: showed in cells that oxidative stress drives fast production of the drug pump P-glycoprotein through a PI3K-AKT-mTORC1-eIF4A route.

Jin P.note: Very common name; identity tied by Southwest University plus co-author Lei Luo. Not the Emory geneticist Peng Jin; do not merge.

Cunningham JT.lab_name: Department of Cancer Biology, University of Cincinnati (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Cunningham JT.role: Cancer biologist who showed in Puigserver's lab at Dana-Farber that mTOR controls mitochondrial activity, later worked on protein synthesis and nucleotide metabolism in cancer in Davide Ruggero's lab at UCSF, and now works at the University of Cincinnati
Cunningham JT.sub: Department of Cancer Biology, University of Cincinnati (PubMed affiliation, 2026) · Department of Urology and Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, UCSF (Davide Ruggero lab, papers 2014–2016) · Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (Puigserver lab, 2007)
story: mTOR is best known for switching on protein production when nutrients are plentiful. In the Atlas study CUN2007, Cunningham and colleagues in Puigserver's lab showed that mTORC1 also runs the cell's power plants, the mitochondria. Working in cultured cells and mouse muscle, they found that mTORC1 helps two proteins, the transcription factor YY1 and its partner PGC-1alpha, switch on genes for mitochondrial function. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin lowered these genes and cut the cells' oxygen use. The paper explains part of why mTOR inhibitors change metabolism, and why long-term rapamycin can affect energy use in tissues.

Cunningham then moved to Davide Ruggero's lab at the University of California, San Francisco. A 2014 first-author paper in Cell showed that the cancer gene Myc couples protein synthesis and nucleotide production through a single enzyme, PRPS2, whose own production is controlled at the translation step. In 2016 Cunningham was a co-author on a method to measure mTORC1 activity in living animals by PET scanning with radioactively labelled transferrin.

A 2026 paper lists Cunningham at the Department of Cancer Biology, University of Cincinnati, on work showing that the enzyme caspase-1 acts as a scaffold that binds raptor, a part of mTORC1, to hold back excess inflammatory NF-kB signalling in leukemia cells. The same mTOR focus and the earlier Ruggero connection tie this record to the same person.

highlights.CUN2007: First author: showed that mTORC1 drives mitochondrial gene expression and oxygen use through a YY1-PGC-1alpha complex, and that rapamycin lowers both.

Cunningham JT.note: Current affiliation (University of Cincinnati) rests on a 2026 PubMed record; tie is topical (mTORC1/raptor) plus the earlier mTOR imaging work, not a shared co-author. Career stage at the time of CUN2007 (student or postdoc) not confirmed. No official page opened (web search budget ran out).

Kusuda T.lab_name: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Kusuda T.role: Rheumatologist and researcher at the University of Tokyo who studies how B cells go wrong in lupus, and first author of the 2026 study tying the arginine sensor CASTOR1 to mTORC1 in antibody-making cells
Kusuda T.sub: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (group of senior author Fujio, 2026) · Department of Medicine and Rheumatology, Tokyo Metropolitan Geriatric Hospital (2023) · Department of Rheumatology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (2016)
story: Cells check whether they have enough of each amino acid before they grow. CASTOR1 is a sensor for the amino acid arginine: when arginine is low, CASTOR1 holds mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in check. In the Atlas study KUS2026, Kusuda and colleagues in the University of Tokyo group of senior author Fujio gave CASTOR1 a clear job in the body. In mice without CASTOR1, mTORC1 was overactive in B cells, the immune cells that make antibodies. The mice made more plasma cells (antibody factories), more antibodies including ones against their own DNA, and developed kidney inflammation like that seen in lupus.

Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. In blood from people with lupus, plasmablasts with less CASTOR1 went with more active disease. That human result is a correlation; the cause-and-effect evidence comes from mice. The study is one of few that link a specific nutrient sensor upstream of mTORC1 to a human autoimmune disease.

PubMed shows Kusuda as a clinician as well as a researcher: a 2016 case report from the Department of Rheumatology at Tokyo Medical and Dental University, and a 2023 letter on COVID-19 vaccination and rheumatoid arthritis in older patients from the Tokyo Metropolitan Geriatric Hospital, with a joint affiliation at the University of Tokyo. Rank and training details could not be confirmed.

highlights.KUS2026: First author: showed in mice that losing the arginine sensor CASTOR1 overactivates mTORC1 in B cells and leads to lupus-like autoantibodies and kidney disease, with a matching correlation in patients.

Kusuda T.note: Group leader named by surname only (last author Fujio K on KUS2026); first name not confirmed from a source. No official page opened.

Shim JH.lab_name: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Seoul, South Korea)
Shim JH.role: Medicinal chemist in Hyeon Soo Kim's group at the Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine, who designs small molecules, and first author of the study of the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH that switches on mTORC1 through Sestrin2
Shim JH.sub: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Hyeon Soo Kim group, papers 2021–2026)
story: Muscle builds protein when mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on, and the amino acid leucine is one of its main triggers. Leucine works by binding a sensor protein called Sestrin2, which then lets go of the brake on mTORC1. In the Atlas study SHIM2026, Shim and colleagues made DLMEH, a modified form of D-leucine (the mirror-image form of normal leucine) designed as a prodrug, a compound the body converts into the active form. DLMEH bound Sestrin2 about as tightly as ordinary leucine and switched on mTORC1 only when Sestrin2 was present.

In human muscle cells grown in a dish, DLMEH restored protein production. In rats whose muscles were wasted by the steroid dexamethasone, it preserved muscle mass, grip strength and endurance. The rat model mimics steroid-induced muscle loss, not age-related sarcopenia, and no human trial has been done.

On PubMed, Shim's papers come from the Department of Anatomy at Korea University College of Medicine with Hyeon Soo Kim and are mostly chemistry: a 2021 paper on a catalyst that builds molecules with a chosen handedness, and a 2026 paper on a new oral pain-relief compound that blocks the Nav1.7 sodium channel in nerve cells. Rank could not be confirmed.

highlights.SHIM2026: First author: designed the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH and showed it activates mTORC1 through Sestrin2, restoring protein synthesis in human muscle cells and preserving muscle in steroid-treated rats.

Shim JH.note: Common Korean name; identity tied by Korea University Department of Anatomy plus co-author Hyeon Soo Kim. No official page opened.

Perera RM.lab_name: Perera Lab, Department of Anatomy, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Perera RM.role: Professor of Anatomy at UCSF whose lab studies how autophagy and the lysosome, the cell's recycling centre, help cancer cells cope with stress, and a co-author of two Science papers on how lysosomal cholesterol switches on mTORC1
Perera RM.sub: Professor of Anatomy and Deborah Cowan Endowed Professor, University of California San Francisco
story: The lysosome is the cell's recycling centre, and its outer surface is also where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. Perera is a co-author of two Atlas studies led by Zoncu that showed cholesterol is one of the nutrients mTORC1 reads there. In CAS2017, the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 was needed for cholesterol to activate mTORC1, and NPC1, the protein that moves cholesterol out of the lysosome, held mTORC1 back. In SHI2022, a lysosomal protein named LYCHOS was identified as a cholesterol sensor: when cholesterol is high it binds and ties up GATOR1, a brake on mTORC1, so mTORC1 can be recruited and switched on. Both are studies in cells.

Perera is a professor in the Department of Anatomy at the University of California San Francisco and holds the Deborah Cowan Endowed Professorship. According to the university profile, the lab studies how autophagy and the lysosome regulate the response to cellular stress in ways that promote cancer progression.

highlights.CAS2017: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9, with NPC1 acting as a brake.
highlights.SHI2022: Co-author: contributed to the identification of LYCHOS as the lysosomal cholesterol sensor that signals to mTORC1 by binding GATOR1.

Perera RM.note: Training (PhD, postdoc) not found on the UCSF profile or lab homepage; left out. Has photo already.

Yu J.lab_name: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, and Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (Tianjin, China)
Yu J.role: Anesthesiology researcher at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital and first author of a mouse study showing that breathing hydrogen gas protects memory after sepsis by calming mTOR in brain support cells
Yu J.sub: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital · Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can damage the brain, and survivors often have long-lasting problems with memory and thinking. In the Atlas study YU2026, Yu and colleagues used a mouse model of sepsis and looked at the medial prefrontal cortex, a brain region for planning and memory. mTOR was overactive there, and this stopped oligodendrocyte precursor cells from maturing into the cells that wrap nerve fibres in myelin, the insulation that speeds up signals. The mice lost myelin and did worse in a water maze memory test.

Breathing a high concentration of hydrogen gas lowered mTOR activity, restored oligodendrocyte maturation and myelin, and improved memory. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, had a similar protective effect, and a drug that switches mTOR on (NV-5138) was used to check the mechanism. For the Atlas, this is an example where too much mTOR activity is harmful in the brain. All of the work was done in mice.

Jiafeng Yu is listed in the Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, and the Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology, in the group of Yang Yu and Yonghao Yu, which has studied hydrogen therapy in sepsis for several years. No other publication could be tied to this name with confidence.

highlights.YU2026: First author: showed in septic mice that mTOR overactivity blocks myelin repair in the prefrontal cortex and that hydrogen gas or rapamycin restores myelin and memory.

Yu J.note: Common surname (Yu J); career history left out because no second identity tie was found.

Yu Yang.lab_name: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital, and Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (Tianjin, China)
Yu Yang.role: Anesthesiologist and researcher at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital who studies hydrogen gas as a treatment for sepsis and its brain damage, and co-senior author of the 2026 study linking hydrogen, mTOR and myelin repair
Yu Yang.sub: Department of Anesthesia, Tianjin Medical University General Hospital · Tianjin Institute of Anesthesiology (papers from at least 2020 to 2026)
story: Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can damage the brain, leaving survivors with memory problems. In the Atlas study YU2026, led by first author Jiafeng Yu with Yang Yu and Yonghao Yu as corresponding authors, septic mice had overactive mTOR in the medial prefrontal cortex. This kept oligodendrocyte precursor cells from maturing into the cells that make myelin, the insulation around nerve fibres, and the mice lost myelin and memory. Breathing high-concentration hydrogen gas lowered mTOR activity, restored myelin and improved memory; rapamycin had a similar effect. The work was done in mice.

Hydrogen gas is studied as a mild antioxidant and anti-inflammatory treatment. On PubMed, Yang Yu appears with Yonghao Yu in the Department of Anesthesiology at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital on earlier hydrogen studies in septic mice, including a 2020 paper showing that hydrogen protected the gut in severe sepsis through the Nrf2 pathway. Rank and training could not be confirmed.

highlights.YU2026: Co-senior (last) author: co-led the mouse study showing that hydrogen gas restores myelin and memory after sepsis by restraining mTOR in the prefrontal cortex.

Yu Yang.note: Very common name; Yang Yu is distinct from Yonghao Yu (same department, also corresponding author on YU2026). The many 'Yu Y' hydrogen papers from Tianjin are mostly Yonghao Yu; only PMID 33463500 was checked for Yang Yu. Do not merge the two.

Goodarzi H.lab_name: Goodarzi Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, University of California, San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Goodarzi H.role: Systems biologist at UCSF and the Arc Institute who combines computation and experiments to find hidden gene-regulation programs that drive cancer, and a co-author of two Atlas studies on mTORC1 in drug-resistant cancers
Goodarzi H.sub: Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, UCSF · Core Investigator, Arc Institute (since 2023) · postdoc in cancer systems biology, Rockefeller University (to 2016) · PhD in computational biology and genomics, Princeton (2010)
story: Goodarzi appears in the Atlas on two cancer studies about mTORC1, the growth-control complex. In MEN2023, the bi-steric inhibitor RMC-6272, which is more than 25 times more selective for mTORC1 than for mTORC2, fully shut down mTORC1, including its control of 4E-BP1, a target that rapamycin only partly blocks. It overcame resistance to hormone therapy and to CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer cells and in tumours grown from patient samples in mice. In YAN2026, from Davide Ruggero's lab, B cell lymphomas that import small protein fragments (dipeptides) through the transporter SLC15A3 kept mTORC1 switched on and resisted the chemotherapy drug 6-mercaptopurine; the resistant tumours became sensitive to rapamycin.

Goodarzi earned a PhD in computational biology and genomics at Princeton in 2010 and did postdoctoral training in cancer systems biology at Rockefeller University, finishing in 2016. According to the UCSF profile, his lab studies how cancer cells reach disordered gene expression states that drive progression, using unbiased computational and experimental methods to find regulatory pathways that are not yet known.
He is a professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at UCSF and has been a Core Investigator at the Arc Institute in Palo Alto since 2023.

highlights.MEN2023: Co-author: contributed to the breast cancer study showing that the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-6272 overcomes hormone-therapy and CDK4/6-inhibitor resistance.
highlights.YAN2026: Co-author: contributed to the lymphoma study showing that SLC15A3-driven dipeptide import keeps mTORC1 on and causes chemotherapy resistance that rapamycin can reverse.

Goodarzi H.note: UCSF profile gives PhD location as Princeton, New Jersey (institution name implied). Profile uses 'his'. Has photo already. Lab website goodarzilab.ucsf.edu listed on profile but not opened; lab_url set to the profile page.
